sourceBasis.syllabus: R-2025 Unit V: casting, forming, machining, joining, CNC, additive manufacturing and smart manufacturing.
prescribedBooks: Jonathan Wickert & Kemper Lewis, An Introduction to Mechanical Engineering, Cengage Learning, 4th Edition, 2016.
R. K. Rajput, Fundamentals of Mechanical Engineering, Laxmi Publications, 2017.
sourceBasis.note: Original ACADRIX study questions based on the syllabus and prescribed-book themes; textbook passages are not reproduced and these are not claimed official PYQs.

questions.a: The process of converting raw materials into useful products with specified shape, size, properties and quality.
A manufacturing process in which molten material is poured into a mould cavity and allowed to solidify.

questions.q: What is a pattern in casting?
questions.a: A replica or form used to create the mould cavity into which molten material is poured.
A cavity or form that gives the required shape to the molten material during casting.

questions.q: Why is a pattern generally made slightly different from the final casting dimensions?
questions.a: To provide necessary allowances for processes such as shrinkage, machining and draft.
The transformation of the molten material into a solid after heat is removed.
An undesired imperfection in a casting that affects its quality, dimensions, appearance or performance.
A manufacturing process in which material is plastically deformed into the desired shape without removing the bulk of the material as chips.
Rolling and forging.
A forming process in which material passes between rotating rolls to reduce thickness or change cross-section.
A forming process in which material is plastically deformed by compressive forces, commonly using dies or hammers/presses.
A forming process in which material is forced through a die opening to produce a continuous product of a desired cross-section.
A manufacturing process in which unwanted material is removed from a workpiece to obtain the required shape, size and surface finish.
A tool with a cutting edge used to remove material from a workpiece during machining.
A machining process in which a rotating workpiece is cut by a tool to produce mainly cylindrical surfaces.
A machining process in which a rotating multi-edge cutter removes material from a workpiece.
A machining operation used primarily to produce or enlarge circular holes using a rotating drill.
An abrasive machining process that removes small amounts of material, commonly for accurate dimensions and surface finish.
The relative speed between the cutting edge and the work surface at the cutting zone.
The relative advancement of the cutting tool or workpiece during machining, specified according to the operation.
The thickness of material removed in one machining pass, measured in the direction normal to the machined surface as defined for the operation.

questions.q: What is a chip in machining?
questions.a: The portion of material removed from a workpiece by a cutting tool.
A manufacturing method used to connect two or more components or parts into an assembly.
Gas welding and arc welding.
A joining process that produces coalescence of materials, commonly using heat, pressure, or a combination of both.
A joining process using a filler metal with a relatively low melting temperature, without melting the base materials in the normal process.
A joining process in which a filler metal is melted and distributed between closely fitted surfaces without melting the base metals.
A joint in which an adhesive material bonds the surfaces of two or more parts.
Computer Numerical Control.
Machining in which machine-tool operations are controlled by programmed numerical instructions executed by a control system.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of CNC over conventional manual control?
questions.a: CNC provides programmable, repeatable and accurate control of machine operations.
The automatic control of a machine or process using coded numerical instructions.
A set of coded instructions that directs a CNC machine to perform specified operations and movements.
A manufacturing approach that builds a component by adding material layer by layer from digital model data.

questions.q: What is another common name for additive manufacturing?
questions.a: 3D printing.

questions.q: What is the basic material-building principle of additive manufacturing?
questions.a: Material is selectively deposited, fused, cured or otherwise formed layer by layer to create the part.

questions.q: What is a digital model in additive manufacturing?
questions.a: A computer-based geometric representation used to define the part to be manufactured.

questions.q: State one advantage of additive manufacturing.
questions.a: It can produce complex geometries that may be difficult or uneconomical to make by conventional processes.
A manufacturing approach that uses connected digital technologies, data, automation and intelligent control to improve manufacturing performance.

questions.q: What is the role of sensors in smart manufacturing?
questions.a: Sensors collect information about machines, processes or products for monitoring, control and analysis.

questions.q: Why is data important in smart manufacturing?
questions.a: Data supports monitoring, analysis, process optimisation, predictive decisions and quality improvement.
The use of control systems and technology to perform manufacturing tasks with reduced direct human intervention.
Manufacturing designed to respond efficiently to changes in product type, quantity or production requirements.

questions.q: Which manufacturing process removes material: casting, forming or machining?
questions.a: Machining.

questions.q: Which manufacturing process primarily adds material layer by layer?
questions.a: Additive manufacturing.

questions.q: Which process uses a mould cavity to obtain the product shape?
questions.a: Casting.

questions.q: Which process plastically deforms material to obtain shape?
questions.a: Forming.

questions.q: What is process selection in manufacturing?
questions.a: Choosing a suitable manufacturing process based on product geometry, material, dimensions, surface finish, quantity, quality, cost and other requirements.

questions.q: Why is surface finish important in manufacturing?
questions.a: It can affect friction, wear, sealing, fatigue performance, appearance and functional performance.
It ensures that manufactured parts satisfy design requirements and fit or function correctly with mating components.
The permitted variation in a specified dimension or characteristic.
Production of large quantities of standardised products using organised and often specialised processes.

questions.q: Why is CNC useful for repeated production?
questions.a: A validated program can repeatedly perform the same programmed operations with consistent control.
The gradual deterioration or loss of cutting-tool material during machining.

questions.q: How can excessive tool wear affect a machined part?
questions.a: It can reduce dimensional accuracy, worsen surface finish and increase cutting forces or heat.

questions.q: What is the purpose of coolant or cutting fluid in machining?
questions.a: It can help control heat and friction, improve tool life and assist chip removal and surface quality, depending on the operation.
A manufacturing approach that produces a part close to its final required shape, reducing subsequent material removal or finishing.

questions.q: What is a manufacturing process plan?
questions.a: An organised sequence of manufacturing operations selected to convert a raw material or blank into the required product.

questions.q: Why should manufacturing safety be considered during process selection?
questions.a: The selected process must be capable of being operated and maintained without exposing people or equipment to unacceptable hazards.

questions.q: What is smart manufacturing intended to improve?
questions.a: Manufacturing performance such as productivity, quality, flexibility, traceability, maintenance and resource efficiency.
